text:
Eigenvalues and eigenvectors sound intimidating for some people who are not familiar with it. But actually the main idea of it starts with something simple: an arrow. When a matrix changes an arrow, some arrows stay on the same line. These are eigenvectors, and their eigenvalues describe how they are scaled.
This can be hard to see when a matrix is introduced as a box of numbers at the first time we saw them. We get busy multiplying entries and lose track of what the calculation does. Here is a picture that maybe can make the idea easier to follow for you.

title: Why Do Some Arrows Stay on the Same Line?
text:
Why this feels unintuitive
A matrix initially looks like a table of numbers. Multiplying it by a vector seems to involve several separate calculations, so it is surprising that the result could be as simple as multiplying the entire vector by one number.
The missing intuition is that a matrix also describes a transformation of space. Different arrows can respond differently to the same transformation. An eigenvector identifies a direction where all that apparent complexity reduces to scaling.
The horizontal and vertical axes are convenient for writing coordinates, but a transformation does not have to treat those axes as special. Its simplest behavior may occur along a diagonal. Finding eigenvectors lets us discover the directions that are special to this particular matrix.

title: Why Do Some Arrows Stay on the Same Line?
text:
Three arrows, one transformation
Consider the matrix \[
A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}.
\] Its rule is straightforward: an arrow ending at \((x,y)\) moves to \((2x+y,x+2y)\). Start with three arrows, all beginning at the origin: \[
\mathbf{w}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\mathbf{v}_1=\begin{pmatrix}1\\1\end{pmatrix},\qquad
\mathbf{v}_2=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix}.
\] Before looking at the figure, predict which arrows will change direction. The following code applies exactly the same matrix to all three.


Show R code
A <- matrix(c(2, 1,
              1, 2), nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)

vectors <- cbind(
  w  = c(1, 0),
  v1 = c(1, 1),
  v2 = c(1, -1)
)

transformed <- A %*% vectors




Show R code
local({
  old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
  on.exit(par(old_par))

  par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(3.8, 3.8, 2.6, 0.8),
      mgp = c(2.3, 0.7, 0), tcl = -0.25, las = 1,
      family = "sans", cex = 0.95)

  colors <- c(w = "#D55E00", v1 = "#0072B2", v2 = "#009E73")

  draw_panel <- function(V, panel_title, labels) {
    plot(NA, xlim = c(-1.4, 3.6), ylim = c(-1.5, 3.5),
         asp = 1, xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i",
         xlab = "x coordinate", ylab = "y coordinate",
         main = panel_title, axes = FALSE)

    abline(h = -1:3, v = -1:3, col = "#E7EBEF", lwd = 0.8)
    abline(h = 0, v = 0, col = "#89939E", lwd = 1)
    abline(a = 0, b = 1, col = "#89939E", lty = 3)
    abline(a = 0, b = -1, col = "#89939E", lty = 3)
    axis(1, at = -1:3)
    axis(2, at = -1:3)
    box(col = "#CBD2D9")

    for (j in seq_len(ncol(V))) {
      arrows(0, 0, V[1, j], V[2, j],
             col = colors[j], lwd = 3, length = 0.12)
    }

    points(0, 0, pch = 16, cex = 0.6)
    text(V[1, 1], V[2, 1] - 0.24, labels[1], cex = 0.9)
    text(V[1, 2] - 0.1, V[2, 2] + 0.23, labels[2],
         adj = c(1, 0.5), cex = 0.9)
    text(V[1, 3] + 0.16, V[2, 3], labels[3],
         adj = c(0, 0.5), cex = 0.9)
  }

  draw_panel(vectors, "Before",
             c("w: (1, 0)", "v1: (1, 1)", "v2: (1, -1)"))
  draw_panel(transformed, "After applying A",
             c("Aw: (2, 1)", "Av1: (3, 3)", "Av2: (1, -1)"))
})





Figure 1: The same matrix acts on three arrows. Colors identify the same arrow before and after the transformation. Both panels use the same coordinate scale; dotted diagonal lines mark the two eigenvector directions.




In Figure 1, the horizontal arrow \(\mathbf{w}\) moves to \((2,1)\), changing both length and direction. Meanwhile, \(\mathbf{v}_1\) moves to \((3,3)\): it becomes three times as long while staying on its original line. The third arrow, \(\mathbf{v}_2\), does not move at all.
These last two arrows are eigenvectors of \(A\). Their eigenvalues are \(3\) and \(1\), respectively. Notice that being an eigenvector does not require an arrow to grow. Staying unchanged is also a scaling operation: multiplication by one.
Eigenvectors can have many different lengths. For example, \((2,2)\) also lies along the first eigenvector direction and becomes \((6,6)\). Any nonzero multiple of \(\mathbf{v}_1\) is another eigenvector with the same eigenvalue. This is why an eigenvector helps identify an entire direction.

title: Why Do Some Arrows Stay on the Same Line?
text:
The equation describes the picture
The definition simply records what we observed:
\[
A\mathbf{v}=\lambda\mathbf{v},\qquad \mathbf{v}\ne\mathbf{0}.
\] Here, \(A\) is the transformation, \(\mathbf{v}\) is an eigenvector, and \(\lambda\) is its eigenvalue. For that vector, applying the matrix has exactly the same effect as multiplying by \(\lambda\).
The zero vector is excluded because it has no direction. A negative eigenvalue reverses the arrow along the same line, while a zero eigenvalue collapses it to the origin. The length multiplier is \(|\lambda|\), so values between zero and one shorten the arrow.
R can verify the eigenvalues directly:


Show R code
eigen_result <- eigen(A, symmetric = TRUE)
eigen_result$values


[1] 3 1

title: Why Do Some Arrows Stay on the Same Line?
section: What happens if we keep going?
text:
What happens if we keep going?
Now repeatedly apply \(A\) to the ordinary arrow \(\mathbf{w}\). Its successive endpoints are
\[
(1,0)\rightarrow(2,1)\rightarrow(5,4)
\rightarrow(14,13)\rightarrow(41,40).
\]
The coordinates become increasingly similar relative to their size. The arrow approaches the \(45\)-degree direction of \(\mathbf{v}_1\).


Show R code
steps <- 0:6
trajectory <- matrix(NA_real_, nrow = 2, ncol = length(steps))
trajectory[, 1] <- vectors[, "w"]

for (i in 2:ncol(trajectory)) {
  trajectory[, i] <- as.vector(A %*% trajectory[, i - 1])
}

angles <- atan2(trajectory[2, ], trajectory[1, ]) * 180 / pi

local({
  old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
  on.exit(par(old_par))

  par(mar = c(4.2, 4.3, 1.1, 1.0), mgp = c(2.6, 0.7, 0),
      tcl = -0.25, las = 1, family = "sans")

  plot(steps, angles, type = "n", xlim = c(-0.15, 6.2),
       ylim = c(-2, 52), xaxs = "i", yaxs = "i",
       xlab = "Number of transformations",
       ylab = "Arrow angle (degrees)", axes = FALSE)

  abline(h = seq(0, 40, 10), v = steps, col = "#E7EBEF", lwd = 0.8)
  abline(h = 45, col = "#65717D", lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  axis(1, at = steps)
  axis(2, at = c(0, 10, 20, 30, 40, 45))
  box(col = "#CBD2D9")

  lines(steps, angles, col = "#0072B2", lwd = 2.5)
  points(steps, angles, col = "#0072B2", pch = 19, cex = 0.9)

  text(3, 49, "Eigenvector direction: 45 degrees", cex = 0.95)
  text(0.15, 3.5, "Start: 0 degrees", adj = c(0, 0.5), cex = 0.9)
  text(6, angles[length(angles)] - 4,
       sprintf("After 6: %.1f degrees", angles[length(angles)]),
       adj = c(1, 0.5), cex = 0.9)
})





Figure 2: Repeated transformations turn the starting arrow toward the 45-degree eigenvector direction. This graph tracks the arrow’s angle, not its length.




Why does this happen? Our starting arrow contains components along both eigenvector directions. Each transformation triples the component along \(\mathbf{v}_1\) and leaves the component along \(\mathbf{v}_2\) unchanged. Eventually, the growing component dominates, explaining the pattern in Figure 2.
The difference between the two coordinates stays at one throughout this sequence. What shrinks is that difference relative to the coordinates themselves. This explains how the arrow can approach a diagonal even though its endpoint never lies exactly on it after any finite number of transformations.
This outcome depends on the starting arrow. One placed exactly along \(\mathbf{v}_2\) would remain there. In this example, the larger eigenvalue reveals the faster-growing mode, but that mode must be present initially to take over.

title: Why Do Some Arrows Stay on the Same Line?
text:
What to remember
An eigenvector reveals a direction where a matrix acts through simple scaling; its eigenvalue describes that scaling. Together, they help explain both an individual transformation and the patterns that can emerge when it is repeated. The arrows that keep their line offer a way to understand the whole transformation

title: Why Do Some Arrows Stay on the Same Line?
text:
A small example
Let’s use this matrix as an example:
\[
A = \begin{pmatrix}2 & 1 \\ 1 & 2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Think of a vector as an arrow starting at the origin. The vector \((1,1)\) ends one unit right and one unit up. This R code for you to see applies the matrix to that arrow. The symbol %*% means matrix multiplication.

A <- matrix(c(2, 1, 1, 2), nrow = 2)
v <- c(1, 1)
A %*% v

     [,1]
[1,]    3
[2,]    3


The result is \((3,3)\). The arrow becomes three times as long, but still points along the same diagonal. That makes \((1,1)\) an eigenvector of \(A\), with an eigenvalue of 3.
Eigenvectors can also have different lengths.For example, an arrow twice as long along this diagonal still gets stretched by three. Its starting size changes, but its eigenvalue stays the same because the scaling is unchanged.

plot(0, 0, type = "n", xlim = c(0, 3.5), ylim = c(0, 3.5),
     xlab = "x", ylab = "y", asp = 1)
arrows(0, 0, 3, 3, col = "red", lwd = 2)
arrows(0, 0, 1, 1, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
text(1, 1, "Before", pos = 2)
text(3, 3, "After", pos = 2)




The blue arrow is the original vector. The red arrow extends three times as far along the same line.




Now try \((1,0)\). This arrow starts out pointing horizontally.

w <- c(1, 0)
A %*% w

     [,1]
[1,]    2
[2,]    1


The result is \((2,1)\), so the arrow tilts upward. It changes direction, which means \((1,0)\) is not an eigenvector of this matrix. The difference is easy to see: one arrow gets longer along its original line, while the other turns.

plot(0, 0, type = "n", xlim = c(0, 3.5), ylim = c(0, 3.5),
     xlab = "x", ylab = "y", asp = 1)
arrows(0, 0, 2, 1, col = "red", lwd = 2)
arrows(0, 0, 1, 0, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
text(1, 0, "Before", pos = 2)
text(2, 1, "After", pos = 2)




One detail matters: an arrow is an eigenvector of a particular matrix. A different matrix might turn that same arrow. So the special relationship is between the arrow and the transformation we apply.

title: Why Do Some Arrows Stay on the Same Line?
text:
What the formula means
The definition puts this observation into one equation:
\[
Av = \lambda v, \qquad v \ne 0.
\]
Here, \(v\) is an eigenvector and \(\lambda\) is its eigenvalue. For this particular vector, multiplying by the matrix does the same thing as multiplying by one number.
An eigenvalue of one leaves the arrow unchanged. A negative eigenvalue reverses it along the same line. An eigenvalue of zero collapses it to the origin. The zero vector itself is excluded because it has no direction.

title: Why Do Some Arrows Stay on the Same Line?
text:
Why this is useful
If we keep applying our matrix to \((1,0)\), we get \((2,1)\), then \((5,4)\), then \((14,13)\). The arrow gets closer to the diagonal direction of \((1,1)\).
That happens because the part along this eigenvector grows faster than the other part. An arrow starting exactly along the other eigenvector, \((1,-1)\), would stay unchanged instead.
Eigenvectors show us special directions within a transformation. Eigenvalues tell us what happens along those directions. Together, they make it easier to understand how a system changes over time.

title: Why Do the Arrows That Stay on the Same Line Matter So Much?
text:
Eigenvalues and eigenvectors sound intimidating for some people who are not familiar with them. But actually the main idea starts with something simple: an arrow. When a matrix changes an arrow, some arrows stay on the same line. These are eigenvectors, and their eigenvalues describe how they are scaled.
This can be hard to see when a matrix is introduced as a box of numbers the first time we see one. We get busy multiplying entries and lose track of what the calculation does.
But even after I got the picture, one thing still bugged me quite a while. These arrows are actually pretty rare. If you take a typical matrix and apply it to a random arrow, the arrow almost always turns. In the plane, these special arrows fill at most two lines. And yet, eigenvectors seem to show up everythere in datascience. OCA uses them, Markov chains use them, and even Google’s original PageRank scores, which Google used to rank webpages, come from an eigenvector. Most explanations I’ve seen on textbooks focus on how to calculate those eigenvectors, not on why these few special arrows are such a big deal.
That is the question I want to figure out in my first blog post: if almost every arrow turns, what do the few arrows that don’t turn tell us about all the other ones? I’ll start with a small example and a picture that may make the idea easier to follow for you. Then we’ll do a little experiment in R and keep applying the sma matrix over and over, a bit like how a Markow chain moves forward one step at a time, and see where the turning arrows end up.

title: What Should I Build Next? What Python Job Postings Suggest
text:
When I started learning Python when I was a freshmen student in college, deciding what to build next was not obvious. Backend development, databases, and machine learning all seemed useful, but I wanted a project with a very clear purpose.
So my question is: what do the topic tags on Python job postings suggest about whether a beginner should start with a backend application or a machine learning project?
But only looking at job postings online cannot tell me which project will get someone hired. They can give me a limited view of the work employers advertise and help me make a more informed learning choice.

title: What Should I Build Next? What Python Job Postings Suggest
text:
Collecting the data
So I decide to use the public Python.org Job Board and collect only its first listing page. Each row represents one listing URL. I will extract the title, location, topic tags, posting dates, and links.
The code I use will have the about the same as our class exercise: read the HTML, select the repeated job cards, and extract one field from each card. A selector tells R which part of the page contains the information.
For ethical collection as required, the code does not bypass logins, CAPTCHAs, paywalls, or other access restrictions. If the website denies access, I would stop collecting.


Code
url <- "https://www.python.org/jobs/"
html_file <- file.path(data_dir, "python_jobs.html")
metadata_file <- file.path(data_dir, "collection_metadata.csv")

# Set it FALSE will reuse the snapshot. If none exists, collect one page.
# I will set it TRUE only if when I want to deliberately collecting a new snapshot.
refresh <- FALSE
new_snapshot <- refresh || !file.exists(html_file)

if (new_snapshot) {
  page <- read_html(url)
} else {
  page <- read_html(html_file)
}

job_cards <- page |> html_elements("ol.list-recent-jobs > li")

if (length(job_cards) == 0) {
  stop("No job cards found. Check the page before continuing.")
}

jobs_raw <- tibble(
  title = job_cards |>
    html_element(".listing-company-name a") |> html_text2(),
  location = job_cards |>
    html_element(".listing-location") |> html_text2(),
  tags = job_cards |>
    html_element(".listing-job-type") |> html_text2(),
  posted_date = job_cards |>
    html_element("time") |> html_attr("datetime"),
  job_url = job_cards |>
    html_element(".listing-company-name a") |> html_attr("href")
)

jobs_raw <- jobs_raw |>
  mutate(job_url = xml2::url_absolute(job_url, url))

if (any(is.na(jobs_raw$title) | str_squish(jobs_raw$title) == "") ||
    any(is.na(jobs_raw$job_url) | jobs_raw$job_url == "")) {
  stop("A title or link is missing. Check the extraction before continuing.")
}

if (new_snapshot) {
  metadata <- tibble(
    source_url = url,
    snapshot_date_utc = format(Sys.time(), "%Y-%m-%d", tz = "UTC"),
    retrieval_method = "Downloaded with rvest::read_html(url)",
    scope = "First listing page only"
  )
  xml2::write_html(page, html_file)
  write_csv(metadata, metadata_file)
} else {
  metadata <- read_csv(metadata_file, show_col_types = FALSE)
}

snapshot_date <- metadata$snapshot_date_utc[1]

# Display the first five collected listings.
knitr::kable(
  jobs_raw |> select(title, location, posted_date) |> head(5),
  col.names = c("Job title", "Location", "Posting date"),
  caption = "First five collected listings"
)

title: What Should I Build Next? What Python Job Postings Suggest
text:
Cleaning the information
Now I want to remove all extra spaces, convert the posting dates, and remove duplicate URLs. I also record which listings have no topic tags. Missing tags are missing information, so they do not show that a job requires none of these skills.
I mainly focus on six broad labels: Back end, Machine Learning, Database, Front end, Cloud, and Web. These are selected topic labels that basically most student want to learn afterwards, and it is not an exhaustive list of employers’ requirements. str_detect() checks whether each label appears, and sum() later counts the TRUE values.


Code
jobs <- jobs_raw |>
  mutate(
    title = str_squish(title),
    location = str_squish(location),
    tags = coalesce(str_squish(tags), ""),
    tags_missing = tags == "",
    posted_date = as.Date(substr(posted_date, 1, 10))
  ) |>
  distinct(job_url, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    backend = str_detect(tags, fixed("Back end", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    machine_learning = str_detect(tags, fixed("Machine Learning", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    database = str_detect(tags, fixed("Database", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    frontend = str_detect(tags, fixed("Front end", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    cloud = str_detect(tags, fixed("Cloud", ignore_case = TRUE)),
    web = str_detect(tags, fixed("Web", ignore_case = TRUE))
  )

#save the cleaned data
write.csv(
  jobs,
  here("blog", "posts", "post2", "data", "jobs_clean.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

#read the saved data for the analysis
jobs <- read.csv(
  here("blog", "posts", "post2", "data", "jobs_clean.csv"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

#convert posting dates back to dates after reading the CSV
jobs$posted_date <- as.Date(jobs$posted_date)

n_total <- nrow(jobs)
n_duplicates <- nrow(jobs_raw) - n_total
n_missing <- sum(jobs$tags_missing)
n_missing_dates <- sum(is.na(jobs$posted_date))
n_missing_locations <- sum(is.na(jobs$location) | jobs$location == "")
n_backend <- sum(jobs$backend)
n_ml <- sum(jobs$machine_learning)
n_both <- sum(jobs$backend & jobs$machine_learning)

#display the cleaning checks.
quality <- tibble(
  Check = c(
    "Job cards extracted",
    "Unique listing URLs",
    "Duplicate URLs removed",
    "Listings without topic tags",
    "Listings with missing dates",
    "Listings with missing locations"
  ),
  Count = c(
    nrow(jobs_raw),
    n_total,
    n_duplicates,
    n_missing,
    n_missing_dates,
    n_missing_locations
  )
)

write.csv(
  quality,
  here("blog", "posts", "post2", "results", "tables", "data_quality.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

  quality,
  caption = "Data checks after cleaning"

title: What Should I Build Next? What Python Job Postings Suggest
text:
Which topics appear most often?


Code
skills <- tibble(
  skill = c("Back end", "Machine Learning", "Database",
            "Front end", "Cloud", "Web"),
  postings = c(n_backend, n_ml, sum(jobs$database),
               sum(jobs$frontend), sum(jobs$cloud), sum(jobs$web))
) |>
  mutate(percent = round(100 * postings / n_total, 1)) |>
  arrange(desc(postings), skill)

write.csv(
  skills,
  here("blog", "posts", "post2", "results", "tables", "skill_summary.csv"),
  row.names = FALSE
)

Do backend and machine learning appear together?

title: What Should I Build Next? What Python Job Postings Suggest
text:
What I would build next
For my next general Python project, I would start with a small backend application. Backend appears at least as often as ML in this sample, so it is a reasonable area to prioritize when choosing between the two.
I would build an application tracker that lets a user add a job application, update its status, and retrieve saved records. Next, I would connect it to a small database and check how it handles missing or invalid inputs.
The overlap also gives me a reason to connect the two areas. For a project that combines both, I could connect the job description classifier to the application tracker and show its prediction through the application. That would let me practice using a model inside a working application.
This is my proposed learning sequence. The listings do not specifically request an application tracker, a particular database, or one framework. The practical decision is about what to build next, not a claim that one project guarantees employment.

title: What Should I Build Next? What Python Job Postings Suggest
text:
Limits of the analysis
This is a small, international sample from the first page of one job board and it is not a random sample of Python jobs. So the employers may appear more than once, and different URLs do not necessarily represent different vacancies.
The tags are broad descriptions rather than a complete reading of each job’s requirements as I did not measure experience requirements, salaries, applicant competition, or hiring outcomes. So, I cannot conclude that the postings are entry level jobs or that learning a frequent topic causes a higher chance of receiving an offer.
The takeaway is to use the frequency and overlap of these tags as one input into a learning decision. Before applying for a role, I would still read the full description and compare its requirements with my experience.

title: Education and Unemployment Through the Pandemic and Recovery
text:
The unemployment rate gives us a quick picture of the job market, but people with different levels of education may have very different experiences. I wanted to look more closely at those differences. How did unemployment vary by education from 2019 to 2024, and does the latest comparison also hold within age groups? I start with 2019 to see where each group stood before the pandemic. Then I look at the change in 2020 and the pattern through 2024. Finally, I compare education groups among people of similar ages. This helps separate a group’s starting unemployment rate from how much its situation changed. ## Data and approach For this post, I use IPUMS CPS Basic Monthly data covering all 72 months from January 2019 through December 2024. I focus on civilians ages 25–64 who are in the labor force. Starting at 25 reduces the influence of people still finishing their initial education, while stopping at 64 limits differences related to retirement. I use four education groups: less than high school, high school or equivalent, some college or an associate’s degree, and a bachelor’s degree or more. The unemployment rate measures unemployed people, including those on temporary layoff, as a share of the labor force. People outside the labor force are left out of that calculation.


Show the R code
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

post_dir <- here("blog", "posts", "post3")

data_file <- file.path(
  post_dir, "data", "cps_2019_2024.csv.gz"
)

results_dir <- file.path(post_dir, "results")

dir.create(
  results_dir,
  showWarnings = FALSE,
  recursive = TRUE
)

stopifnot(file.exists(data_file))

cps_raw <- read_csv(
  data_file,
  col_select = c(YEAR, MONTH, ASECFLAG, AGE, EDUC, EMPSTAT, WTFINL),
  col_types = cols(.default = col_double()),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)

stopifnot(nrow(problems(cps_raw)) == 0)
stopifnot(sum(cps_raw$ASECFLAG == 1, na.rm = TRUE) == 0)
#want to check every requested year and month is present.
cps_raw <- cps_raw |> filter(YEAR %in% 2019:2024)
month_check <- cps_raw |> distinct(YEAR, MONTH)
stopifnot(
  nrow(month_check) == 72,
  all(month_check$MONTH %in% 1:12)
)
education_order <- c(
  "Less than high school", "High school",
  "Some college / associate", "Bachelor's or more"
)
# keep those employed and unemployed adults
cps_eligible <- cps_raw |>
  filter(AGE >= 25, AGE <= 64, EMPSTAT %in% c(10, 12, 20, 21, 22))

cps <- cps_eligible |>
  mutate(
    education = case_when(
      EDUC >= 2 & EDUC <= 71 ~ "Less than high school",
      EDUC == 73 ~ "High school",
      EDUC %in% c(81, 91, 92) ~ "Some college / associate",
      EDUC %in% c(111, 123, 124, 125) ~ "Bachelor's or more",
      TRUE ~ NA_character_
    ),
    education = factor(education, levels = education_order),
    unemployed = EMPSTAT %in% c(20, 21, 22),
    age_group = case_when(
      AGE <= 34 ~ "25–34",
      AGE <= 44 ~ "35–44",
      AGE <= 54 ~ "45–54",
      TRUE ~ "55–64"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(education), !is.na(WTFINL), is.finite(WTFINL), WTFINL > 0)
excluded_n <- nrow(cps_eligible) - nrow(cps)
#the formula for annual unemployment rate is: 100 x weighted unemployed / weighted labor force.
#Pooling all 12 months makes this a ratio of annual-average population totals.
annual <- cps |>
  group_by(YEAR, education) |>
  summarise(
    observations = n(),
    months = n_distinct(MONTH),
    unemployment_rate = 100 * sum(WTFINL * unemployed) / sum(WTFINL),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
#we require all four education groups in each year, with all 12 months.
stopifnot(
  nrow(annual) == 24,
  all(annual$months == 12),
  all(annual$unemployment_rate >= 0 & annual$unemployment_rate <= 100)
)
#Figure 2: use pivot_wider() to put 2019 and 2020 on the same row.
shock <- annual |>
  filter(YEAR %in% c(2019, 2020)) |>
  select(education, YEAR, unemployment_rate) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = YEAR, values_from = unemployment_rate, names_prefix = "rate_"
  ) |>
  mutate(change_pp = rate_2020 - rate_2019)
#Figure 3: calculate the same weighted rate within four age groups in 2024.
by_age <- cps |>
  filter(YEAR == 2024) |>
  group_by(YEAR, age_group, education) |>
  summarise(
    observations = n(),
    months = n_distinct(MONTH),
    unemployment_rate = 100 * sum(WTFINL * unemployed) / sum(WTFINL),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
stopifnot(nrow(by_age) == 16, all(by_age$months == 12))
#stacks the three summary tables.
all_results <- bind_rows(
  annual |> mutate(result = "annual_rates"),
  shock |> mutate(result = "change_2019_2020"),
  by_age |> mutate(result = "age_rates_2024")
)
write_csv(all_results, file.path(results_dir, "summary_results.csv"))
#make the displayed numbers easier to read.
comparison <- annual |>
  select(YEAR, education, unemployment_rate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = education, values_from = unemployment_rate)
baseline <- comparison |> filter(YEAR == 2019)
latest <- comparison |> filter(YEAR == 2024)
hs_change <- shock$change_pp[shock$education == "High school"]
college_change <- shock$change_pp[shock$education == "Bachelor's or more"]
age_comparison <- by_age |>
  select(age_group, education, unemployment_rate) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = education, values_from = unemployment_rate)
age_count <- sum(age_comparison$`High school` > age_comparison$`Bachelor's or more`)
change_description <- if_else(
  hs_change > college_change,
  "The high school group saw the larger change in its unemployment rate.",
  "The high school group's change was no larger than the college group's."
)
takeaway <- if_else(
  latest$`High school` > latest$`Bachelor's or more`,
  "In 2024, unemployment was lower among people with at least a bachelor's degree than among those whose highest qualification was high school.",
  "In 2024, having at least a bachelor's degree was not associated with a lower unemployment rate than having only a high school diploma."
)
#use the same source note and figure dimensions throughout the post.
source_note <- "Source: IPUMS CPS, University of Minnesota. Weighted using WTFINL."
knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 9, fig.height = 5.5, dpi = 150)


After cleaning, I have 2,992,422 person-month records. I leave out 0 otherwise eligible records because their education or weight cannot be used. The CPS interviews some people in several months, so the record count includes repeat interviews. Each respondent represents a different number of people. To account for that, I use the WTFINL weight recommended by IPUMS. For each group and year, I add up the weighted unemployed and divide by the weighted labor force, then multiply by 100. Pooling all 12 months gives the ratio of annual-average totals. I do not apply seasonal adjustment. ## 1. How did the education groups move over time?


Show the R code
figure1 <- ggplot(
  annual,
  aes(x = YEAR, y = unemployment_rate)
) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ education, ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2019:2024) +
  scale_y_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "Unemployment by education, 2019–2024",
    subtitle = "Civilian labor-force participants ages 25–64; identical axes",
    x = NULL, y = "Annual unemployment rate (%)",
    caption = source_note
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
figure1





Show the R code
ggsave(file.path(results_dir, "figure1_trend.png"), figure1,
       width = 9, height = 5.5, dpi = 300)


I first look at the full six-year picture. In 2019, unemployment was 3.8% among people with only a high school diploma, compared with 2.1% among those with at least a bachelor’s degree. In 2024, those rates were 4.4% and 2.3%. Each panel uses the same scale, so we can compare both the levels and the paths over time. The next figure looks directly at how much each group changed in 2020. ## 2. How large was the change in 2020?


Show the R code
figure2 <- ggplot(shock, aes(x = change_pp, y = education)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "The change in unemployment from 2019 to 2020",
    subtitle = "Annual rate in 2020 minus annual rate in 2019; ages 25–64",
    x = "Change in percentage points", y = NULL,
    caption = source_note
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
figure2





Show the R code
ggsave(file.path(results_dir, "figure2_change.png"), figure2,
       width = 9, height = 5.5, dpi = 300)


To make the 2020 change easier to compare, I subtract each group’s 2019 rate from its 2020 rate. The change was 5.3 percentage points for the high school group and 2.7 points for the bachelor’s-or-more group. The high school group saw the larger change in its unemployment rate. For context, going from 4% to 7% would be a three-percentage-point increase. These changes describe the groups’ unemployment rates; they do not track which individual workers lost jobs. ## 3. Does the latest comparison hold within age groups?


Show the R code
figure3 <- ggplot(by_age, aes(x = unemployment_rate, y = education)) +
  geom_point(size = 3, color = "steelblue") +
  facet_wrap(~ age_group, ncol = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, NA)) +
  labs(
    title = "Unemployment by education within age groups",
    subtitle = "2024 annual rates; civilian labor-force participants; identical axes",
    x = "Unemployment rate (%)", y = NULL,
    caption = source_note
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
figure3





Show the R code
ggsave(file.path(results_dir, "figure3_age.png"), figure3,
       width = 9, height = 7, dpi = 300)


I also wanted to check whether the overall comparison holds among people of similar ages. In 2024, the high school group had higher unemployment than the bachelor’s-or-more group in 4 of the four age groups. Breaking the results down this way shows where the overall pattern holds and where it does not. People within an age group can still have different backgrounds and jobs, so this does not remove every possible explanation for the gap. ## How I read these results I would be careful about saying education alone caused these differences. People with different qualifications also work in different occupations, industries, and places. The analysis leaves out people outside the labor force, and IPUMS reports pandemic-era nonresponse and employment-status misclassification. I keep the reported classifications. I also do not calculate confidence intervals that account for the survey design, so I would not read too much into small gaps. My takeaway: In 2024, unemployment was lower among people with at least a bachelor’s degree than among those whose highest qualification was high school. Looking at the trend, the change in 2020, and the age groups gives a fuller picture of how unemployment differed across education levels. These comparisons help describe who was struggling in the job market, while leaving open the question of how much of the difference education itself explains. Data source: IPUMS CPS, University of Minnesota. Variable definitions: EDUC, EMPSTAT, and WTFINL. All analysis code appears in this post; the repository README provides replication instructions.

title: Why Do the Arrows That Stay on the Same Line Matter So Much?
section: So where do the turning arrows go?
text:
So where do the turning arrows go?
If we keep applying our matrix to \((1,0)\), we get \((2,1)\), then \((5,4)\), then \((14,13)\). The arrow gets closer to the diagonal direction of \((1,1)\). But how close, and how fast? Let’s track it. The code below applies \(A\) six times and measures the angle between the arrow and the diagonal line through \((1,1)\) after each step.

# Angle, in degrees, between an arrow and the diagonal line through (1, 1)
angle_to_diagonal <- function(v) {
  # size of the part along (1, 1)
  along  <- abs(v[1] + v[2]) / sqrt(2)
  # size of the part along (1, -1)
  across <- abs(v[1] - v[2]) / sqrt(2)  
  atan2(across, along) * 180 / pi
}

v <- c(1, 0)
trajectory <- data.frame()
for (step in 0:6) {
  trajectory <- rbind(trajectory,
                      data.frame(step = step, x = v[1], y = v[2],
                                 angle = angle_to_diagonal(v)))
  v <- as.vector(A %*% v)
}
knitr::kable(trajectory, digits = 2,
             col.names = c("Step", "x", "y", "Angle to diagonal (degrees)"))




Step

The angle starts at 45 degrees and drops below a tenth of a degree after just six steps. And if you look at the numbers closely, there’s a pattern. After the first step, each angle is about three times smaller than the one before it: 18.43, 6.34, 2.12, 0.71. Why three?
That happens because the part along the eigenvector \((1,1)\) grows faster than the other part. Here’s what I mean: we can split any arrow into two pieces: one piece along \((1,1)\) and one piece along the other eigenvector of \(A\), which is \((1,-1)\). For example, \((1,0)\) is just half of \((1,1)\) plus half of \((1,-1)\). Every time we apply \(A\), the \((1,1)\) piece gets multiplied by its eigenvalue, 3, and the \((1,-1)\) piece gets multiplied by its eigenvalue, 1, so it doesn’t change at all. After \(k\) steps we get
\[
A^k \begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 0\end{pmatrix} = \frac{3^k}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1 \\ 1\end{pmatrix} + \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}1 \\ -1\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Every step, the \((1,1)\) piece gets three times bigger compared to the other piece, so the arrow leans more and more toward the diagonal. That’s where the three comes from. It’s just the ratio of the two eigenvalues, 3 divided by 1.
At this point I wondered if \((1,0)\) was just a lucky choice. To check, I tried sixteen arrows pointing in all different directions. I applied \(A\) to each of them five times, and then shrank every arrow back to length one so we only compare directions.

directions <- seq(0, 337.5, by = 22.5) * pi / 180
# one arrow per column
before <- rbind(cos(directions), sin(directions))

after <- before
for (step in 1:5) after <- A %*% after
# rescale to length one
after <- sweep(after, 2, sqrt(colSums(after^2)), "/")  

# the two arrows that start exactly along the other eigenvector, (1, -1)
on_other_line <- abs(before[1, ] + before[2, ]) < 1e-8
arrow_col <- ifelse(on_other_line, "#CD6600", "blue")

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
panels <- list(before, after)
titles <- c("Before", "After applying A five times")
for (i in 1:2) {
  plot(0, 0, type = "n", xlim = c(-1.1, 1.1), ylim = c(-1.1, 1.1),
       xlab = "x", ylab = "y", asp = 1, main = titles[i])
  abline(0, 1, lty = 2, col = "gray50")
  arrows(0, 0, panels[[i]][1, ], panels[[i]][2, ],
         col = arrow_col, lwd = 2, length = 0.08)
}




Left: sixteen arrows before applying A. Right: the same arrows after applying A five times, rescaled to length one. The blue arrows all end up on the dashed diagonal line. The two orange arrows start on the line through (1, -1) and stay there.




It wasn’t luck. Fourteen of the sixteen arrows end up on the diagonal line. Some point toward \((1,1)\) and some toward \((-1,-1)\), but it’s the same line. The only two that don’t are the orange ones. An arrow starting exactly along the other eigenvector, \((1,-1)\), would stay unchanged instead, because its eigenvalue is 1. But these two only survive because they start exactly on that line. If you push one of them even a tiny bit off of it, that tiny piece along \((1,1)\) gets tripled every step, and eventually it takes over too.

title: Why Do the Arrows That Stay on the Same Line Matter So Much?
section: Does it matter how far apart the eigenvalues are?
text:
Does it matter how far apart the eigenvalues are?
If the three really comes from dividing the two eigenvalues, then the speed should change when the eigenvalues get closer together. I wanted to check this, so I made a second matrix, \(B\). It has the same eigenvectors as \(A\), and its biggest eigenvalue is still 3. The only difference is that its other eigenvalue is 2.7 instead of 1:
\[
B = \begin{pmatrix}2.85 & 0.15 \\ 0.15 & 2.85\end{pmatrix}.
\]

B <- matrix(c(2.85, 0.15, 0.15, 2.85), nrow = 2)
eigen(A)$values

[1] 3 1

eigen(B)$values

[1] 3.0 2.7


R confirms it: \(A\) has eigenvalues 3 and 1, and \(B\) has 3 and 2.7. Now let’s start both matrices from \((1,0)\), apply each one 40 times, and watch the angle.

track_angle <- function(M, v, n_steps) {
  angles <- numeric(n_steps + 1)
  for (k in 0:n_steps) {
    angles[k + 1] <- angle_to_diagonal(v)
    v <- as.vector(M %*% v)
  }
  angles
}

steps <- 0:40
angle_A <- track_angle(A, c(1, 0), 40)
angle_B <- track_angle(B, c(1, 0), 40)

# First step at which the arrow is within one degree of the diagonal
c(A = min(steps[angle_A < 1]), B = min(steps[angle_B < 1]))

 A  B 
 4 39 



plot(steps, angle_B, type = "l", col = "red", lwd = 2, ylim = c(0, 45),
     xlab = "Number of times the matrix is applied",
     ylab = "Angle to diagonal (degrees)")
lines(steps, angle_A, col = "blue", lwd = 2)
abline(h = 1, lty = 2, col = "gray50")
text(2.3, 7.5, "A", pos = 4)
text(12, 19, "B", pos = 4)
legend("topright", legend = c("A: eigenvalues 3 and 1", "B: eigenvalues 3 and 2.7"),
       col = c("blue", "red"), lwd = 2, bty = "n")




How far the arrow is from the diagonal after each step, starting from (1, 0). The dashed line marks one degree. A gets there after 4 steps, while B needs 39.




This was the part that surprised me the most. Both matrices stretch \((1,1)\) by exactly 3, so if you only looked at the biggest eigenvalue, you would think they behave the same. They don’t. With \(A\), the arrow is within one degree of the diagonal after 4 steps. With \(B\), it takes 39 steps, almost ten times longer. The reason is the same as before: each step, the \((1,1)\) piece gains on the other piece by the ratio of the eigenvalues. For \(A\) that ratio is \(3/1 = 3\), but for \(B\) it is only \(3/2.7 \approx 1.11\). That’s why, with \(B\), the arrow keeps “remembering” where it started for so long.

title: Why Do the Arrows That Stay on the Same Line Matter So Much?
text:
What I learned from this
Eigenvectors show us special directions within a transformation. Eigenvalues tell us what happens along those directions. Together, they make it easier to understand how a system changes over time. That’s the textbook summary, and it’s true, but it felt pretty abstract to me until I actually ran these experiments. Two things finally clicked.
The first is that eigenvectors are not just weird exceptions. I used to think of them as the few arrows that happen not to turn. But if you apply the same matrix again and again, almost every arrow ends up lining up with the eigenvector that has the biggest eigenvalue. So the eigenvector is basically telling you where everything is heading. I think this is why eigenvectors show up in Markov chains and PageRank. In both cases, what we care about is where a process ends up after many steps, and that answer is an eigenvector. Even for PCA, one classic way to find the first principal component, called the power method, uses the same trick of multiplying by a matrix (the covariance matrix) over and over.
The second is that computing the eigenvalues isn’t enough. We should also compare them. The biggest eigenvalue tells us which direction wins in the end, but how close the second one is to the biggest tells us how long that takes. With 3 and 1 it took 4 steps; with 3 and 2.7 it took 39. I find it helpful to think about this with a labor market example. In a simple model where workers move between having a job and being unemployed each month, this ratio decides whether a jump in unemployment fades in a few months or sticks around for a long time.
One thing we need to be careful about, though: this only works when one eigenvalue is strictly bigger in size than all the others. For example, a matrix that rotates every arrow by 90 degrees has no real eigenvectors at all, so the arrows just keep spinning around and never settle on any line.
So, back to my question. The few arrows that don’t turn matter because they tell us where all the other arrows are going, and the eigenvalues tell us how fast they get there. For me, that’s a much more useful way to think about eigenvectors than just remembering \(Av = \lambda v\).

title: Did Paychecks Keep Up With Prices?
text:
In 2022 it felt like everyone I knew was complaining about prices: rent, groceries, gas. But a lot of people also got big raises around the same time. So which one won?
My question: since COVID started, have paychecks kept up with prices, and did some industries do better than others?
This matters because the number on your paycheck isn’t really what you live on. If your pay goes up 10% but prices go up 15%, you can buy less than before. Economists call the paycheck number the nominal wage and what it can buy the real wage. The real wage is the one people actually feel.

title: Did Paychecks Keep Up With Prices?
text:
Data
All my data comes from FRED, the St. Louis Fed’s database, which gets it from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. I use average hourly earnings for all private-sector workers (CES0500000003), the same series for 13 industries, and the Consumer Price Index (CPIAUCSL). Everything is monthly and seasonally adjusted.
I compare February 2020, the last month before COVID hit, with August 2026, the newest month that has both wages and prices. My code downloads each series from FRED the first time it runs and saves a copy in data/raw/, so the results don’t change every time I render.


Code
import os
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

for folder in ["data/raw", "data/processed", "results/figures", "results/tables"]:
    os.makedirs(folder, exist_ok=True)

# download a series from FRED once, then reuse the saved csv
def get_fred(series_id):
    path = "data/raw/" + series_id + ".csv"
    if not os.path.exists(path):
        url = "https://fred.stlouisfed.org/graph/fredgraph.csv?id=" + series_id
        pd.read_csv(url).to_csv(path, index=False)
    df = pd.read_csv(path)
    df.columns = ["date", "value"]
    df["date"] = pd.to_datetime(df["date"])
    return df

wages = get_fred("CES0500000003").rename(columns={"value": "wage"})
cpi = get_fred("CPIAUCSL").rename(columns={"value": "cpi"})

title: Did Paychecks Keep Up With Prices?
text:
Adjusting for inflation
To compare pay across years, I turned every month’s wage into August 2026 dollars:
real wage = wage * CPI(Aug 2026) / CPI(that month)
I also calculated 12-month growth rates for wages and prices, which is how inflation is usually reported in the news.


Code
df = wages.merge(cpi, on="date")

# growth compared to the same month last year (%)
df["wage_growth"] = (df["wage"] / df["wage"].shift(12) - 1) * 100
df["inflation"] = (df["cpi"] / df["cpi"].shift(12) - 1) * 100

# keep Jan 2019 to Aug 2026
df = df[(df["date"] >= "2019-01-01") & (df["date"] <= "2026-08-01")].copy()

# real wage in August 2026 dollars
latest_cpi = df["cpi"].iloc[-1]
df["real_wage"] = df["wage"] * latest_cpi / df["cpi"]

df.to_csv("data/processed/wages_cpi_clean.csv", index=False)

# any missing months?
df[df["cpi"].isna()]


          date   wage  cpi  wage_growth  inflation  real_wage
235 2025-10-01  36.85  NaN      3.91991        NaN        NaN


One thing I noticed: October 2025 has no CPI. The government shutdown stopped BLS from collecting prices that month, so I left it blank instead of making up a number. That’s why the lines have a small gap.

title: Did Paychecks Keep Up With Prices?
text:
What I found


Code
feb20 = df[df["date"] == "2020-02-01"].iloc[0]
aug26 = df[df["date"] == "2026-08-01"].iloc[0]

pay_change = (aug26["wage"] / feb20["wage"] - 1) * 100
price_change = (aug26["cpi"] / feb20["cpi"] - 1) * 100
real_change = (aug26["real_wage"] / feb20["real_wage"] - 1) * 100

summary = pd.DataFrame({
    "measure": ["pay change (%)", "price change (%)", "real pay change (%)"],
    "value": [pay_change, price_change, real_change]
}).round(1)
summary.to_csv("results/tables/summary.csv", index=False)
summary


               measure  value
0       pay change (%)   32.3
1     price change (%)   28.9
2  real pay change (%)    2.7


Since February 2020, average pay went up 32.3%. That sounds great until you see that prices went up 28.9% too. So the real raise is only about 2.7% over six and a half years.


Code
plt.figure(figsize=(8, 5))
plt.plot(df["date"], df["wage"], color="gray", label="Actual pay")
plt.plot(df["date"], df["real_wage"], color="tab:blue", label="Pay in August 2026 dollars")
plt.title("Average hourly pay, actual vs. adjusted for inflation")
plt.ylabel("Dollars per hour")
plt.legend()
plt.savefig("results/figures/fig1_real_wage.png", dpi=300)
plt.show()





Source: BLS via FRED (CES0500000003, CPIAUCSL).




The gray line is the actual paycheck: $28.54 an hour in February 2020 and $37.76 in August 2026. The blue line shows what that pay can buy, and it’s much flatter. In today’s dollars, the February 2020 wage was worth $36.78, so the real gain is less than a dollar an hour.
The jump in spring 2020 isn’t a raise. Millions of low-paid workers lost their jobs, so the average pay of the people still working shot up. After that, real pay slid during the inflation surge and bottomed out in June 2022, a bit below where it started.

Think of this chart as a race. When the orange line is above the blue one, prices are growing faster than pay, and I shaded those months. Inflation peaked at 9.0% in June 2022 (the famous 9.1% is the number before seasonal adjustment). Wages grew around 5% a year, which wasn’t enough, and prices won every month from April 2021 to April 2023. After that, wages pulled ahead again, but since April 2026 prices have been slightly ahead once more.

industries = {
    "Mining and logging": "CES1000000003",
    "Construction": "CES2000000003",
    "Manufacturing": "CES3000000003",
    "Wholesale trade": "CES4142000003",
    "Retail trade": "CES4200000003",
    "Transportation": "CES4300000003",
    "Utilities": "CES4422000003",
    "Information": "CES5000000003",
    "Financial activities": "CES5500000003",
    "Professional services": "CES6000000003",
    "Education and health": "CES6500000003",
    "Leisure and hospitality": "CES7000000003",
    "Other services": "CES8000000003",
}

price_ratio = aug26["cpi"] / feb20["cpi"]

rows = []
for name, series_id in industries.items():
    ind = get_fred(series_id)
    start = ind[ind["date"] == "2020-02-01"]["value"].iloc[0]
    end = ind[ind["date"] == "2026-08-01"]["value"].iloc[0]
    change = ((end / start) / price_ratio - 1) * 100
    rows.append([name, start, end, round(change, 1)])

by_industry = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["industry", "wage_feb2020", "wage_aug2026", "real_change"])
by_industry = by_industry.sort_values("real_change")
by_industry.to_csv("results/tables/real_change_by_industry.csv", index=False)

plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6))
bars = plt.barh(by_industry["industry"], by_industry["real_change"], color="tab:blue")
plt.bar_label(bars, fmt="%.1f", padding=3)
plt.axvline(0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
plt.margins(x=0.15)
plt.title("Change in real hourly pay by industry, Feb 2020 to Aug 2026")
plt.xlabel("Percent")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig("results/figures/fig3_industries.png", dpi=300)
plt.show()





Source: BLS via FRED (average hourly earnings by industry, CPIAUCSL).




Almost every industry came out a little ahead, but leisure and hospitality (restaurants, hotels, bars) stands out at +9.0%. It was also the lowest-paid industry before COVID, at $16.92 an hour, and it probably raised pay the most because these businesses had a hard time hiring when things reopened in 2021. Mining and logging (-5.6%) and wholesale trade (-2.7%) were the only ones that fell behind.

title: Did Paychecks Keep Up With Prices?
text:
Limits
These are averages, so they don’t describe every worker, and they only cover hourly pay, not benefits, hours, or taxes. The CPI is also an average basket, so your own inflation could be higher or lower. And this is descriptive: it shows what happened, not exactly why.

title: Did Paychecks Keep Up With Prices?
text:
Takeaway
So, did paychecks keep up? Yes, but barely. Pay rose 32.3% and prices rose 28.9%, which leaves a real raise of about 2.7%, less than a dollar an hour. Workers fell behind for two years during the inflation surge, slowly caught up, and lower-paid industries like restaurants and hotels did best. If your raise felt like it disappeared at the grocery store, you weren’t imagining it.
The code, data, and charts are all in my GitHub repo, and the README explains how to rerun everything.
